entry.title: The WIP Limit Isn’t the Problem

link.title: The WIP Limit Isn’t the Problem

entry.content:
In an earlier post I described a mismatch: I want slow, deliberate, many-voiced feedback before work starts, and fast, unambiguous, solitary feedback once it does. The resolution was that these aren’t contradictory preferences — they’re the same principle, matching the feedback mechanism to whichever oracle can actually answer the question at that stage. Human judgement for direction. The system for execution.

There’s a related tension I’ve watched play out repeatedly on a small team, and it doesn’t resolve the same way. It looks, on the surface, like a scheduling problem. It isn’t.

The oscillation

The pattern goes roughly like this. The team takes on too many workstreams at once — not because anyone mis-scoped the sprint, but because everybody wants something of their own to work on, or believes their thing is the higher priority, despite that not really being their call to make. So the sprint ends up planned as a mixture, a bit of everything, to keep everyone satisfied going in.

Inevitably, little of it finishes cleanly. People are pulled out of their own work constantly — into code review, into testing sessions, into implementation discussions for streams they’re not even driving — and by the end of the sprint nobody has actually finished anything. What does get finished is rushed across the line in the last day or two.

So the retrospective conclusion is sensible: focus on less. Reduce WIP. The next sprint, people pair or mob rather than each running their own stream.

And then a different problem shows up. Only one person can drive at a time. The others — the navigators — get bored. They start quietly working on side things during the session, less engaged, present but not really there. The work does get finished on time this time. But people feel flat about it. Demotivated. Under-stretched. Convinced more could have been achieved.

So the next retrospective says: let’s take on more, give people their own things again. And the cycle restarts.

Why this isn’t a WIP problem

The obvious read is that the team hasn’t found the right WIP limit yet — too high causes thrashing, too low causes disengagement, so somewhere in between must be correct. I don’t think that’s right, and there’s a tell in the pattern that gives it away: it’s frequently the same people, unhappy in both states. The person complaining “I never get to finish anything, everything’s rushed” in the high-WIP sprint is often the same person complaining “I’m bored, I’m not really contributing” in the paired sprint.

If WIP were the actual variable, you wouldn’t expect that. You’d expect the complaints to come from different people depending on their tolerance for context-switching versus their tolerance for close collaboration. Instead the same individuals are dissatisfied on both sides of the dial, which suggests the dial isn’t what they actually care about.

What they’re asking for, in both states, looks like the same underlying thing: individual, attributable ownership of a solved problem. Something they drove, that’s recognisably theirs, that demonstrates the specific expertise they bring to the team. High WIP gives everyone a shot at that — their own stream, their own area — but not the completion of it, because constant interruption means nothing actually gets finished under their name. Pairing gives the completion, but only to whoever’s driving that session; the navigator gets the outcome without the authorship.

Neither format is failing at its stated job, either. Throughput-wise, the low-WIP sprints work — the team said as much, work gets done on time. What’s failing is a need nobody’s named out loud in the retrospective, because “reduce WIP” and “pair more” are the only vocabulary a sprint retrospective tends to offer. Recognition and demonstrated individual expertise aren’t on that menu, so the dissatisfaction keeps getting misdiagnosed as a process setting, and the process gets nudged back and forth in search of a value that isn’t on that axis at all.

It’s the same shape of mistake as the oracle mismatch from the earlier post, one level up: using a process mechanism — a WIP limit, a pairing cadence — to solve a need that mechanism was never built to answer. A WIP limit is a good tool for managing flow efficiency and reducing thrash. It has no lever for felt ownership. Turning the dial harder in either direction won’t produce a value it was never designed to hold.

Where “shaping” fits, and where it doesn’t yet

This team has already tried, independently, to address a version of this — worth mentioning, because it’s evidence the diagnosis isn’t invented after the fact. We’ve been experimenting with a shaping model rather than conventional planning: a rotating pair kicks off each initiative with a lightweight outline, the relevant specialists feed in asynchronously by area, a short huddle resolves anything unclear, and the facilitator role — whoever drives that shaping — rotates each time rather than defaulting to the same person.

The intent lines up closely with the diagnosis above. Rotating the facilitator role exists specifically so ownership of direction doesn’t collapse onto one person, and so people get turns leading rather than only ever being told what to build by some fixed authority. That’s a genuine, structural answer to part of the ownership problem — at the design stage.

But it’s a partial answer, not a full one, because it operates entirely upstream of the point where the oscillation actually happens. Shaping answers “who got heard on the plan, and who’s facilitating it.” It doesn’t yet answer “who gets to drive — and finish, under their own name — the implementation.” A team can rotate shaping facilitators well and still hit the exact same pairing-versus-solo tension once building starts, because that tension lives entirely in execution, which shaping doesn’t touch. The gap this post is describing sits downstream of everything shaping currently covers.

What would actually close the gap

If the diagnosis is right, the fix isn’t a better WIP number, and it isn’t more or less pairing as a blanket policy. It’s treating ownership itself as something to be deliberately distributed across the roadmap over time — giving each person a stream they drive end-to-end some of the time, and pairing or mobbing at other times, rather than picking one mode as “how we work now” and applying it uniformly until it stops working and gets swapped for its opposite.

Concretely, that might look like extending the same rotation instinct that shaping already applies to facilitation, into execution: an explicit “who owns driving this through to done” decision made once at the start of an initiative, visible to the team, changing initiative to initiative — rather than an implicit, unnamed scramble for it that shows up as either too many parallel streams or too many bored navigators, depending on which way the last retrospective nudged the dial.

That’s a bigger change than adjusting a WIP limit, and it’s probably a harder one to get agreement on — which is exactly why the team needs to see the diagnosis clearly first. Turning the dial feels like doing something. Naming what the dial can’t fix is less comfortable, but it’s the only version of this conversation that stops it from repeating next sprint.

Why driver rotation rarely survives contact with reality

There’s a smaller-scale version of the same tension worth naming, because it complicates the conclusion rather than just illustrating it. Pairing’s usual answer to navigator boredom is to rotate the driver frequently. In practice this rarely happens without real discipline enforcing it, and the reasons are structural, not laziness. Natural stopping points are genuinely hard to find mid-problem, and driving isn’t just operating the keyboard — it’s holding the shape of a half-built solution in your head. Handing that off mid-thought means someone else either preserves your intent or quietly replaces it with their own, and watching your own partially-built approach get overridden while you can only observe is a real discomfort, not reluctance to share credit. Rotate too eagerly and the rotation destroys the very ownership it was meant to produce.

There’s also a genuine efficiency case against it: “I could do this faster if I were just allowed to drive” is frequently true in the moment. What it discounts is that the return on letting someone else drive shows up later, as team capability, rather than now, as this task’s completion time — the same mistake as everything else here, just measuring the wrong feedback loop. Left unmanaged, the loop you can feel immediately wins by default over the one that actually matters. And sometimes there simply isn’t slack to spend on anyone’s growth right now, and some work is genuinely better driven by whoever’s fastest at it.

None of that undermines the point above. Rotation isn’t something that should happen mechanically, on principle, at every opportunity — it’s a deliberate default, consciously overridden when the cost of slowing down is genuinely too high, rather than something that silently never happens because nobody wanted to insist on it. That’s the actual difference between a team managing this tension on purpose and one stuck oscillating through it by accident.
entry.summary: A team oscillating between too much WIP and too much pairing isn't failing to find the right process setting — it's trying to solve a need for individual ownership using a dial that was never built to hold it.

entry.title: Matching the Feedback Loop to the Question

link.title: Matching the Feedback Loop to the Question

entry.content:
I recently worked out why I find infrastructure and platform work so satisfying: it rewards fast, unambiguous, non-negotiable feedback over slow consensus. The system either works or it doesn’t, and it tells you which almost immediately, without needing a committee to agree first.

Then I noticed I hold what looks like the exact opposite view about how work should move through a delivery process — inception, planning, feedback, refinement, estimation, prioritisation, delivery. There, I want the slow version. I want deep conversation early. I want to be genuinely confident we’re building the correct thing, at the correct time, in the correct order, before anyone writes a line of code. Only once work actually begins do I want the fast, harsh, solitary feedback back.

At first glance that looks like holding two contradictory preferences. I don’t think it is. I think it’s one preference, applied correctly to two different kinds of question.

Two different questions, two different oracles

Any piece of work contains at least two distinct questions, and they are answered by different mechanisms.

The first is whether we’re building the correct thing, for the correct reason, at the correct time, in the correct order. There is no protocol for this. No kernel, no compiler, no test suite can tell you whether the feature you’re about to build solves the right problem, or whether now is the right time to build it, or whether it should come before or after some other piece of work. The only oracle for this class of question is other people’s judgement and context — the salesperson who knows what the customer actually asked for, the engineer who remembers why the last attempt at this failed, the person who knows a dependency is landing next quarter that changes the whole calculus. Getting this wrong is expensive, but it’s cheap to get right, because at this stage a wrong assumption costs a conversation, not a rewrite. Slow, many-voiced deliberation isn’t a tax paid here — it’s the mechanism by which correctness gets produced, because there’s no other oracle to consult.

The second is whether this implementation is correct. Once the what and why are settled, this question has a different, better oracle: the system itself. Does the code compile. Does the protocol negotiate correctly. Does the cluster schedule the workload. Does the test pass. This oracle is faster than any committee and can’t be argued with or politely disagreed with over Slack. Continuing to seek consensus here — re-litigating direction mid-implementation, holding design-by-committee meetings about something the compiler already has an opinion on — is now pure cost. The question that needed people has already been answered; what’s left needs a system.

The actual principle

So the shape of the preference isn’t “fast feedback good, slow feedback bad”, or its inverse. It’s to match the feedback mechanism to whichever oracle can actually answer the question at that stage of the work.

Before work starts, the only available oracle is human judgement, so that’s where the deliberation belongs. Once work starts, a better and faster oracle becomes available — the system itself — so that’s where the deliberation should move to. Getting this backwards produces two recognisable failure modes, in opposite directions.

Skip the discovery conversation, and everyone builds fast, locally consistent, collectively wrong things. Each engineer’s individual work might have excellent, unambiguous feedback loops — the code works, the tests pass — but the team has quietly built four different unreconciled interpretations of what “the feature” was supposed to be, and nobody notices until integration, or until it ships to a customer who asked for something else entirely. There are mechanisms to mitigate this, but that’s out of scope here.

Keep having the discovery conversation once work has started, and you get stalled implementation instead. People start re-arguing direction mid-build, because the habit of deliberation never learned when to stop. The system already has an opinion — the tests are failing, the integration doesn’t work — and instead of listening to it, the team keeps convening. That’s design-by-committee applied to a question the compiler already answered.

Both look, from a distance, like “too much” or “too little” process. They’re the same mistake, just consulting the wrong oracle for the question in front of you.

It was never about speed

“Be slow up front, be fast later” is the wrong summary — it would misfire the next time the shape of the problem changed. The principle is about which mechanism is capable of producing a correct answer to whichever question is actually being asked at that point. Early on, that mechanism is conversation, because nothing else can see the context a person can see. Later, it’s the system, because nothing argues with a protocol and wins.

Wanting deep, many-voiced deliberation during planning and wanting to work entirely alone against an unambiguous system once work begins were never in tension. They’re the same judgement, applied correctly twice, to two different questions that happen to sit next to each other in the same piece of work.
entry.summary: Wanting slow, many-voiced feedback before work starts and fast, solitary feedback once it does isn't a contradiction — it's the same preference applied to two different questions.

entry.title: Why Infrastructure Work Feels Different
entry.content:
I’m an application developer by trade. I ended up working in infrastructure and platform engineering out of necessity — someone had to run the Kubernetes cluster, someone had to own the cloud account — and somewhere along the way it became the work I love most. It took me a long time to work out why.

It isn’t a shortage of opinions

The easy answer is that infrastructure has fewer valid ways to do something. Networking works a particular way. The Linux kernel works a particular way. Stray from the accepted approach and things simply stop working. Application development, by contrast, seems to have too many opinions — endless ways to skin the same cat, and teams that spend real time arguing about which way is correct.

I believed this for a while, and it’s half right at best. Infrastructure isn’t actually short of opinions. Ask five platform engineers how to structure a multi-tenant Kubernetes cluster, whether to run a service mesh, how secrets should be managed, or what your GitOps topology should look like, and you’ll get five confidently different answers — argued with exactly the same intensity as any application development debate about state management or dependency injection.

So “fewer opinions” doesn’t hold up. The real difference isn’t the number of valid designs — it’s that the failure mode is legible.

Get a BGP configuration wrong, and routes don’t propagate. Get kernel cgroup settings wrong, and the container gets OOM-killed. The system tells you, unambiguously and quickly, that you were wrong. There’s no room for the failure to be argued away, reframed, or attributed to taste.

A bad abstraction in an application codebase doesn’t page anyone at 3am. It doesn’t fail loudly. It just slowly makes the codebase worse, in a way that’s contestable — someone can always argue it’s fine, or that the real problem is somewhere else, or that it’s a matter of preference. Correctness in application architecture is often adjudicated by consensus, because there’s no kernel standing over the code ready to reject it. What I actually value, then, isn’t a smaller solution space. It’s fast, harsh, non-negotiable feedback — the system either works or it doesn’t, and it tells you which almost immediately.

Domain modelling that’s already done for you

I tend to approach architecture through domain modelling first — trying to understand the shape of the problem before writing anything. I think this is a large part of why infrastructure work resonates so strongly with me specifically.

In infrastructure, the domain model is very often already correct before I arrive. The model for how a TCP handshake works isn’t up for negotiation. Someone solved that decades ago, rigorously, and it’s simply true. My job is to discover and apply that model correctly, not to invent it.

In application development, I’m frequently the one who has to invent the domain model — extracted from a messy, ambiguous, and often contested business reality. And once I’ve built that model, other people get a vote on whether it’s right, because there’s no external authority to appeal to. One of these is discovery. The other is invention under scrutiny. They are very different postures to hold day to day, and I know which one I find more restful.

Why infrastructure work is easier to do alone

There’s a related observation worth separating out, because it looks like the same claim but isn’t: infrastructure work is often easier to solo. The task is clear, and the solution is often just as clear, or more so.

It would be tempting to say this is because the problems are simpler. They’re not. It’s because the blast radius of a decision is usually bounded and observable. I can make a call, ship it, and watch metrics tell me within minutes or hours whether I was right — without first needing four other people to sign off. Application architecture decisions frequently can’t be validated that fast; the consequences of a wrong choice surface weeks or months later, diffused across a codebase multiple people touch. When feedback is slow, consensus becomes a substitute for it — you get agreement up front because you can’t get proof. Slow feedback loops breed committees. Fast feedback loops let one competent person simply get on with it.

The prediction this makes — and where it holds

If this theory is right, it makes a testable prediction: the parts of platform work that are most application-development-flavoured should feel less satisfying than the deep infrastructure layer, because that’s exactly where the fast, legible feedback disappears again. Designing the API for an internal developer platform, or deciding whether something should be a CRD or a Helm chart, has no protocol standing behind it ready to say “wrong.” It’s a design decision, adjudicated by taste and consensus, just like application architecture.

That prediction holds for me. I enjoy that layer of work too — but noticeably less than the deep infrastructure layer beneath it. Which suggests the feedback-loop explanation is doing the real work here, not the “fewer opinions” explanation I started with.

Discovery, not invention under scrutiny

Infrastructure work rewards being right quickly rather than persuasive slowly. The domain is already correctly modelled by physics and protocol, so the work is discovery rather than invention-under-scrutiny. And because the blast radius of most decisions is bounded and observable, it’s possible to act alone and let the system itself settle arguments that would otherwise need a committee.

That’s a satisfying way to spend a working day. It’s also, as it turns out, exactly the wrong way to spend the working days before the work begins — which is a different problem, and one I’ll get to separately.
entry.summary: Infrastructure work isn't satisfying because it has fewer valid designs — it's satisfying because the failure mode is legible, and the feedback is fast enough to work alone.

entry.title: Complacency is the Enemy of Security

link.title: Complacency is the Enemy of Security

entry.content:
A particular kind of institutional blindness sets in when nothing has gone wrong for a while. It isn’t laziness, and it isn’t negligence in any obvious sense — it’s the slow, unannounced erosion of urgency that comes from an absence of consequences. Security has a name for this: complacency, and I think it’s more dangerous than most organisations are willing to admit, because it doesn’t look like a decision. It looks like the absence of one.

How it actually sets in

The organisations that suffer the worst security failures are rarely the ones that never thought about security. More often they’re the ones that thought about it once, set up reasonable foundations, shipped the product, watched it run without incident, and quietly stopped thinking about it. Over time, the absence of visible harm gets treated as evidence of safety, which it isn’t — it’s only evidence that harm hasn’t happened yet. The same pattern shows up well outside software: a driver who’s taken the same route for years without incident eases off the margins, a business that’s never had a fire stops testing the extinguishers.

What a disclosure is actually telling you

Security researchers find holes, report them through whatever disclosure process exists, and move on. Most engineering teams treat that report as a closed incident: fix shipped, researcher thanked, ticket closed. What gets missed is the more useful question underneath it — if someone with the skill and the inclination to look found this, what else is sitting there unfound? A researcher who discloses responsibly represents a narrow slice of the population capable of finding the same class of problem; treating their report as the whole story, rather than a sample of it, is usually where the complacency becomes visible from the outside.

What it looks like day to day

It rarely announces itself as a decision to deprioritise security. It looks like smaller, more reasonable-sounding things: a hardening task that keeps losing to something more urgent every sprint, a credential rotation that keeps getting deferred because coordinating it is annoying and nothing’s gone wrong yet, service-to-service trust that’s never been tightened because nobody’s had the time. None of this is unusual — most engineering organisations carry some version of it. The question worth asking isn’t whether that debt exists, but whether it’s being treated as inert or as compounding. Security debt compounds the same way any other technical debt does, except the interest is paid in an incident rather than in slower builds.

The asymmetry that makes this expensive to get wrong

Security has a structural asymmetry that complacent organisations tend not to sit with: you have to get it right every time, and an attacker only has to get it right once. Your organisation has a roadmap, competing priorities, and finite attention; an attacker has one objective and no sprint cycle to answer to. That asymmetry means the cost of complacency doesn’t accrue smoothly — it accumulates silently and then discharges all at once, at a time of the attacker’s choosing rather than yours. Reactive security work, done under that kind of pressure, costs considerably more than the same work done proactively — in engineering time, in trust, and sometimes in regulatory exposure.

This is also what makes security different from most other categories of product risk. Defer a performance fix and you see it in response times. Defer a UX fix and you see it in conversion. The feedback loop is tight enough to self-correct. Security’s feedback loop is either years long or instantaneous and severe, with very little in between — which means waiting for evidence that the risk is real is, in practice, waiting for the incident itself.

What the alternative actually looks like

The organisations with the strongest security posture aren’t the ones that recovered fastest from a breach — they’re the ones that treated the work as continuous and unglamorous, including during the quiet periods when nothing was obviously on fire. That’s a harder habit to sustain than it sounds, because there’s no natural internal pressure keeping it alive once the original incident that prompted the foundations fades from memory. It has to be maintained deliberately, as a standing property of how the organisation works, rather than revisited only when something forces the question.

The uncomfortable part is that most engineering leaders already know which items on their own backlog are this kind of risk — the credential hygiene that needs attention, the access that hasn’t been audited in a while. The honest question isn’t whether those things carry risk; everyone involved already knows they do. It’s whether the organisation treats security as something actively maintained, or as a state it’s passively in until proven otherwise.
entry.summary: The organisations that get hurt worst by security failures are rarely the ones that never thought about security — they're the ones that thought about it once, then stopped.

entry.title: AI-Generated Code Doesn’t Change What Good Delivery Looks Like

link.title: AI-Generated Code Doesn’t Change What Good Delivery Looks Like

entry.content:
There’s an idea doing the rounds that because AI can generate code faster than any team, the bottleneck in software delivery has moved: code is now cheap, even disposable, and the real constraint is understanding, evaluating and governing it. I think that’s largely correct, but it carries an assumption worth pulling apart: that the infrastructure underneath the software can absorb whatever gets thrown at it. It can’t, not without deliberate design, and the people who’ll feel that first aren’t developers — it’s whoever is responsible for keeping things running while the velocity of change accelerates around them.

Code as something you throw away

Chad Fowler’s Phoenix Architecture series makes the case that the durable part of a system isn’t its implementation, it’s the evaluations that define correctness: the interfaces, the behavioural contracts, the tests that would still hold if the whole thing were rewritten in a different language. Code, on this view, is closer to cache than to capital — a materialised view of intent that’s fine to discard and regenerate, provided the intent itself is written down somewhere that survives the rewrite.

None of this is actually new. Experienced engineers have always known that the most expensive code is the code you keep, and rewrites have always been underrated relative to their reputation. What’s new is the pace this cycle can now turn at, and the volume it can produce while turning.

Where the strain actually lands

When the rate of change goes up, something has to absorb it, and that something is the deployment target — the platform, the infrastructure that accepts artefacts and runs them. On a fleet of hand-provisioned servers, each with its own accumulated quirks and institutional knowledge, every deployment is a small negotiation with the specific machine it’s landing on. That friction has historically been self-limiting: snowflakes accumulate, runbooks grow, and the rate of change slows to match what the platform can actually absorb.

Generative AI doesn’t reduce that friction. It bypasses it at the application layer while leaving it completely intact underneath, which widens the gap between how fast software can be produced and how safely it can be deployed. Platform teams end up facing more deployments, more varied workloads, less consistent artefact quality, and more pressure to move quickly, without any corresponding change to the infrastructure complexity they’re managing. Historically, what gives first under that pressure is operational discipline.

The infrastructure for this already exists

The useful part is that the industry has spent over a decade building the answer to this, for entirely unrelated reasons: scale, reliability, cost, and the general desire to stop treating infrastructure like a collection of pets. The underlying idea was to make the unit of deployment portable and self-describing, so the artefact stops depending on the specifics of the machine it runs on.

Containers are that idea, implemented. They changed operations less because process isolation was technically novel — it wasn’t — and more because they changed the contract between development and operations: a container image is a promise that running it will produce the described behaviour, on any machine that honours the contract. That’s precisely the property regenerative software needs. If implementations are going to be thrown away and regenerated at pace, the deployment target needs to be indifferent to exactly what it’s running — whether a given version was written by a person, generated by a model, or some mixture of both.

Kubernetes is the same idea at orchestration scale. Strip away the operational complexity around it and what’s left is a system for expressing desired state and continuously reconciling reality against it: three replicas, this much memory and CPU, reachable at this address, replaced automatically if unhealthy. That reconciliation loop doesn’t care how the new version was produced — rolling out a hand-crafted release and rolling out one generated overnight are the same operation to the scheduler. Teams running mature Kubernetes platforms are, as a direct consequence, structurally ready for AI-accelerated delivery in a way that teams without one aren’t: the primitives built to absorb human-authored churn are the same primitives that absorb AI-authored churn.

The seam needs more discipline, not less

The corollary Fowler’s argument doesn’t quite spell out is that the seam between disposable code and durable platform needs more care than either side individually — the health checks, resource declarations, shutdown behaviour, privilege model and image construction that make up the container contract. In human-authored software, violations of that contract accumulate slowly enough that a team notices during an incident and fixes it; the feedback loop is long but it works. Under AI-accelerated delivery, the volume crossing that seam goes up enough that violations stop accumulating slowly and start arriving in batches.

Which means the right response to AI-driven velocity isn’t to relax platform discipline, it’s to enforce it earlier and more systematically — not as a gate that slows delivery, but as the contract that makes the platform’s indifference to what it’s running sustainable in the first place.

The point

The teams that come through this well won’t be the ones generating the most code. They’ll be the ones who already invested in a deployment target capable of accepting, validating and running whatever gets generated, quickly and repeatedly. That investment predates AI by a decade and was made for entirely different reasons — scale, reliability, cost. AI hasn’t created the need for it. It’s just made ignoring it considerably more expensive.
entry.summary: If implementations are about to become disposable, the thing that has to absorb the churn is the platform underneath them — and most platforms aren't built for that yet.

entry.title: Structuring Terraform Ownership in Layers
entry.content:
Infrastructure teams tend to discover the same problem at different points in their growth. Someone adds a resource to the wrong workspace, a plan runs against the wrong state file, and suddenly you are staring at a proposed deletion of something critical. The instinct is to consolidate — one workspace, one state file, one place where everything lives. That instinct is wrong.

The right model comes from asking a different question entirely: who should be allowed to change this?

Infrastructure is not flat

Cloud infrastructure has a natural hierarchy. Some resources are foundational — the identity pools, the folder structure, the organisation policies that govern what is even possible within your environment. Others are shared services: a Kubernetes cluster, a database, a message queue that multiple teams depend upon. Others still are workload-specific, tightly coupled to a single application and owned entirely by the team that builds it.

Treating all of these as equivalent, managed from the same workspace with the same credentials, collapses a meaningful distinction. It also maximises blast radius. When a workspace can touch everything, a mistake anywhere can affect everything.

The layered model addresses this by decomposing Terraform configuration into four tiers, each with its own workspace, its own service account, and its own permission boundary.

The four tiers

Organisation is the root. It owns the trust infrastructure that all subsequent automation depends upon: the Workload Identity Pools that allow CI/CD pipelines to authenticate without long-lived keys, the folder hierarchy that structures the environment, and the organisation-wide policies that define what is permissible across every project beneath them. Custom IAM roles that other layers will later reference are also defined here.

What the Organisation workspace does not own is general service account management. It establishes the rules of the game. Everything else belongs to a layer above it.

Governance owns the containers. In GCP, a project is a hard isolation boundary — a separate IAM namespace, a separate quota domain, a separate unit of billing. Creating a project is an administrative act that precedes everything else, and it lives in the Governance workspace. This layer also creates the service accounts and IAM principals that Platform and Delivery teams will later assume when provisioning resources or running workloads.

The separation of project administration from project tenancy is one of the more important principles in this model. The team deploying an application should not also hold the ability to modify the IAM bindings that govern access to the project it runs in.

In AWS, the equivalent isolation boundary is an account rather than a project. The Governance workspace would own account vending through AWS Organizations and the IAM roles that downstream workloads assume via cross-account trust. The concept is identical; only the resource types differ.

Platform owns shared services. Kubernetes clusters, networking, DNS zones, shared image repositories — the infrastructure that Delivery teams depend upon but should not be able to modify directly. Changes here require platform team involvement. Application teams are consumers, not owners.

Delivery is where software reaches customers. Application services, deployment configuration, workload-specific storage — these live in Delivery workspaces, owned and operated by the teams that build the products. They operate with autonomy within their layer because the layers below have already established the boundaries within which that autonomy is safe.

Data sources as contracts

Shared Terraform state is a coupling mechanism. A workspace that can read another workspace’s state file can read everything in it, and often ends up depending on implementation details that were never intended as a public interface.

The better pattern is the data source. Rather than sharing state, a lower layer promises to maintain a resource with a known name. An upper layer looks that resource up.

# Delivery workspace — references a DNS zone it does not own
data "google_dns_managed_zone" "private" {
  name = "services-private"
}

resource "google_dns_record_set" "app" {
  name         = "my-service.${data.google_dns_managed_zone.private.dns_name}"
  managed_zone = data.google_dns_managed_zone.private.name
  type         = "A"
  ttl          = 300
  rrdatas      = [google_compute_address.app.address]
}

The Delivery workspace’s service account holds roles/dns.resourceRecordSetsOwner — enough to manage records within the zone, but not to create, delete, or reconfigure it. The data source lookup requires only roles/dns.reader. The zone is the Platform team’s contract to maintain; the records within it are the Delivery team’s concern.

The same applies to service accounts. A Delivery workspace that needs to assign an identity to a workload does not create that identity — it looks it up.

# Delivery workspace — uses an identity it does not manage
data "google_service_account" "app" {
  account_id = "my-application"
}

resource "google_cloud_run_v2_service" "app" {
  name     = "my-application"
  location = "europe-west2"

  template {
    service_account = data.google_service_account.app.email
  }
}

The service account was provisioned in the Governance workspace. The Delivery workspace can reference it and assign it to a workload. It cannot modify the account’s permissions or create accounts alongside it.

IAM follows the same shape

The layered model maps directly onto the roles held by each workspace’s service account.

Workspace Owns Example roles
Organisation WIPs, folder structure, org policies, custom roles roles/iam.organizationRoleAdmin, roles/orgpolicy.policyAdmin
Governance Projects, billing, service accounts, IAM principals roles/resourcemanager.projectCreator, roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin
Platform Kubernetes clusters, DNS zones, shared networking roles/container.admin, roles/dns.admin, roles/compute.networkAdmin
Delivery Application services, workload-specific records and buckets roles/run.admin, roles/dns.resourceRecordSetsOwner

Within any given layer, per-concern service accounts are preferable to team-level shared accounts. A single platform-sa with broad permissions creates invisible contention — in GCP, quota attribution operates per service account, and a shared account makes that attribution opaque. Scoped accounts like artifact-registry-administrator-sa also limit the damage if a credential is compromised.

Keyless authentication completes the picture

Scoped service accounts are the right unit of identity, but long-lived keys undermine the model regardless of how carefully you scope them. A static key grants persistent access. The natural complement to layered workspaces is Workload Identity Federation — short-lived OIDC credentials that a CI/CD pipeline assumes for the duration of a job and cannot hold beyond it.

In GCP, a dedicated identity project managed by the Organisation workspace hosts Workload Identity Pools for Terraform Cloud and GitHub Actions alike.

# Organisation workspace — establishes the federation trust
resource "google_iam_workload_identity_pool" "tfc" {
  workload_identity_pool_id = "terraform-cloud"
}

resource "google_iam_workload_identity_pool_provider" "tfc" {
  workload_identity_pool_id          = google_iam_workload_identity_pool.tfc.workload_identity_pool_id
  workload_identity_pool_provider_id = "tfc-provider"

  oidc {
    issuer_uri = "https://app.terraform.io"
  }

  attribute_mapping = {
    "google.subject"                   = "assertion.sub"
    "attribute.terraform_workspace_id" = "assertion.terraform_workspace_id"
  }
}

Workspace-specific attribute conditions on IAM bindings ensure that each Terraform Cloud workspace can only assume its designated service account. The Delivery workspace cannot escalate to Governance credentials. The trust boundary is enforced at the identity layer, not by convention.

One nuance: for elevated workspaces — Organisation and Governance — retaining service account impersonation rather than direct WIF principal binding preserves iam.serviceAccounts.actAs as an explicit control point and produces cleaner audit trails. For lower-privilege workspaces, direct binding is simpler. A hybrid approach is sensible; the choice of where to draw that line is a function of your audit requirements.

Blast radius is the real metric

The value of this model is not architectural elegance. It is bounded failure.

When something goes wrong in a Delivery workspace, the damage is contained to that workspace’s resources. A misconfigured count expression cannot delete a VPC. A terraform destroy run against the wrong directory cannot revoke the IAM bindings the entire platform depends upon. The blast radius of a change is determined by what the executing credential can touch — not by what you intended to change.

This is why the boundaries matter across repositories too, not just within Terraform workspaces. A workspace that combines Kubernetes configuration with general configuration management has a larger blast radius than two workspaces that each do one thing. The discipline of separation is not overhead. It is the mechanism by which a mistake stays local.

This scales down as well as up

It is easy to read a four-tier model and conclude it only makes sense with a dedicated platform team and significant organisational complexity. That conclusion is wrong.

A team of two engineers benefits from the separation. When you are working on a delivery task, the confidence that terraform apply cannot inadvertently destroy shared infrastructure is not a luxury — it is what lets you move at speed without anxiety. The layers are not bureaucracy. They are the thing that makes autonomy safe.

The practical starting point for a small team is two workspaces: one combining Organisation and Governance concerns with elevated permissions, and one combining Platform and Delivery resources that reference the foundation via data sources. The four-tier model is the natural destination as the infrastructure and team grow. It does not need to be the starting point.

Least privilege, applied to tooling

The layered model is the principle of least privilege applied to infrastructure tooling rather than to IAM policy alone. Every workspace holds exactly the access it needs to do its job.

A misconfigured plan in a workspace with too-broad permissions can cause damage that takes hours to unpick. The same misconfiguration in a tightly-scoped workspace fails immediately, with a permissions error that tells you exactly what went wrong.

Noisy, local failures are the goal.
entry.summary: Why a flat Terraform workspace maximises blast radius, and how a four-tier ownership model bounds it instead.

entry.title: Building Truly Cross-Functional Teams: Beyond the Frontend-Backend Divide

link.title: Building Truly Cross-Functional Teams: Beyond the Frontend-Backend Divide

entry.content:
The rest of this series has been about technical defaults: client-side architecture, utility-first CSS, progressive enhancement. None of those choices are made in a vacuum — they both shape and get shaped by how teams are organised. This last article is about the organisational side: the frontend/backend split, why it hardened into something closer to a permanent structure than a practical division of labour, and whether it’s still worth what it costs.

Why the split happened

The split had legitimate origins. Early browsers were inconsistent enough that cross-browser CSS and JavaScript were genuinely specialist knowledge. Backend systems carried real complexity of their own — databases, transactions, business logic. The full stack, in the early days, was large enough that very few people could hold all of it well at once. Specialising made sense.

What’s changed isn’t that the stack got smaller. It’s that the gap between “frontend” and “backend” skill, for most applications, has narrowed considerably — partly because the technical choices argued for earlier in this series (server-rendered HTML, HTMX instead of a bespoke client framework, CSS that doesn’t require a build step to reason about) reduce how much there is to specialise in on either side.

What the split actually costs

A JSON API between two teams is a contract, and every contract has to be negotiated, documented, and renegotiated whenever requirements change — which, on any live product, is constantly. I’ve sat in meetings discussing the shape of an API that would have taken less time to simply build, had one person been able to see the whole path from request to rendered page.

The split also sets up two teams to optimise for different things by default: a frontend team under pressure to ship visual polish, a backend team under pressure to protect data integrity and system reliability. Both are legitimate priorities. Split across two teams with two reporting lines and two sets of metrics, they stop being complementary and start being competing, not because the priorities are actually in conflict, but because nobody on either side is accountable for reconciling them.

The subtler cost is what it implies about who’s allowed to know what. Once “frontend” and “backend” become job titles rather than areas of emphasis, developers are discouraged from learning past the boundary, features can’t be shipped end-to-end by one person, and context gets lost every time work crosses the line between teams. None of this is because the underlying material is actually too hard to learn across — most of software engineering’s ideas transfer across the boundary just fine. It’s an organisational habit, not a cognitive limit.

What I’d build instead

A cross-functional team, in the sense I mean it, isn’t a frontend developer and a backend developer sat at the same desk. It’s a team that owns features end-to-end, where most members have both some depth and some breadth — T-shaped, in the usual phrase — and where specialisation, where it exists, is contextual rather than a permanent label. The team is organised around a business domain, not a technical layer, which matters because it’s domains, not layers, that actually change when the product changes.

The technical choices from earlier in this series make this easier to sustain, not just philosophically compatible with it. Server-rendered HTML with HTMX narrows the actual skill gap between “frontend” and “backend” work. CSS without a utility-class compiler step is something any team member can safely touch. Progressive enhancement creates a natural layering — HTML, then CSS, then JavaScript — that maps cleanly onto how much depth a given change actually needs, rather than requiring every change to pass through a framework-shaped lens regardless of its size.

The objections worth taking seriously

The strongest counter-argument is that specialists are more efficient at narrowly defined tasks, which is true, but it undercounts the coordination cost of getting two specialists’ narrow work to meet in the middle. A slightly slower generalist who ships a feature end-to-end is often faster, measured from idea to production, than two specialists who are individually faster but have to synchronise.

The second objection — that full-stack developers capable of this are rare — is real but somewhat self-inflicted. Narrow job descriptions and permanently separated teams actively discourage people from building the breadth this model needs. Hiring and structuring for it is a longer-term fix than hiring around it, but it’s the one that actually closes the gap rather than permanently working around it.

The third is that some developers genuinely prefer to specialise, which I don’t think this model denies anyone. A CSS specialist on a cross-functional team is still a specialist; the difference is that their work stays connected to the rest of the feature because the team, not an API boundary, is the unit of ownership.

Where this series lands

Across these five articles the thread has been the same: start from the primitive that already solves the problem — HTML, HTTP, the cascade — and add complexity only where it’s actually earned. Technically, that means favouring hypertext over bespoke client architecture, favouring the cascade over utility classes, and favouring progressive enhancement over JavaScript-first defaults. Organisationally, it means the frontend/backend split is worth questioning for the same reason: it was the right answer to a technical gap that, for a lot of applications, no longer exists at the size it used to.
entry.summary: The technical arguments earlier in this series point at an organisational one — that the frontend/backend split costs more than it buys once the technical gap it was defending narrows.

entry.title: Progressive Enhancement in the Modern Web: Building Resilient Applications

link.title: Progressive Enhancement in the Modern Web: Building Resilient Applications

entry.content:
The previous two articles argued against defaults — client-heavy architecture, utility-first styling — that trade a foundation for convenience. This one is about the principle that, in my view, should have stayed the default all along: progressive enhancement.

What it actually means

Progressive enhancement starts with semantic HTML that works with nothing else, adds CSS to make it look right, and adds JavaScript last, to make it behave better. The point isn’t nostalgia for simpler interfaces — it’s that if any layer fails to load, the layer beneath it still works. A page built this way degrades; a page built JavaScript-first, with HTML as an afterthought generated at runtime, doesn’t degrade, it just breaks.

A search box, built up in layers

Start with a form that needs nothing but HTTP:

<form action="/search" method="get">
  <label for="search">Search:</label>
  <input type="search" id="search" name="q">
  <button type="submit">Search</button>
</form>

This works everywhere, is indexable, and needs no explanation. Now add autocomplete with HTMX and Alpine:

<form action="/search" method="get">
  <label for="search">Search:</label>
  <input
    type="search"
    id="search"
    name="q"
    hx-get="/api/suggestions"
    hx-trigger="keyup delay:500ms"
    hx-target="#suggestions"
    x-data="{ query: '' }"
    x-model="query"
  >
  <button type="submit">Search</button>
  <div id="suggestions"></div>
</form>

Every keystroke now fires a debounced request to /api/suggestions, and the response fills the suggestions div. Crucially, if that endpoint is slow, broken, or the HTMX script fails to load entirely, the form hasn’t lost anything — it still submits, the server still returns results, the user still searches. Autocomplete was added, not substituted for the thing it’s enhancing.

Pushing further with hx-boost:

<form action="/search" method="get" hx-boost="true">
  <label for="search">Search:</label>
  <input
    type="search"
    id="search"
    name="q"
    hx-get="/api/suggestions"
    hx-trigger="keyup delay:500ms"
    hx-target="#suggestions"
    x-data="{ query: '' }"
    x-model="query"
    hx-indicator=".spinner"
  >
  <button type="submit">Search</button>
  <div class="spinner" style="display:none;">Loading...</div>
  <div id="suggestions"></div>
</form>

Now even the form submission itself avoids a full page reload. The same guarantee holds: strip away HTMX and the form reverts to the plain version a few paragraphs up, not to nothing.

Why this still matters when “everyone has JavaScript”

The usual objection is that JavaScript failure is a theoretical concern — practically every visitor has it enabled. That’s beside the point. Scripts fail to load over flaky mobile connections, get mangled by corporate proxies, collide with browser extensions, or simply throw on a browser nobody tested against. Progressive enhancement isn’t about supporting JavaScript-disabled browsers; it’s about not betting the entire interface on a layer that fails for ordinary, unglamorous reasons on a long enough tail of requests.

It’s also not slower to build, in my experience — it’s slower to build badly, the first time, because it forces you to settle what the feature actually does before deciding how to make it nicer. Teams that skip that step end up debugging edge cases in the JavaScript layer that wouldn’t exist if the HTML layer had been made to work first.

HTML and HTTP already do most of this

Forms, links, and the full range of HTTP methods are underused primitives. A plain <form> gives you validation, keyboard navigation, accessibility, and autofill for free; a plain <a> gives you history, middle-click, right-click, and keyboard navigation for free. HTMX’s contribution isn’t replacing these — it’s extending them to methods HTML forms don’t natively support:

<button hx-delete="/items/1" hx-target="#items-list">
  Delete Item
</button>

That’s still a request/response cycle against a URL; HTMX just lets the button issue a DELETE instead of forcing the page through a form that only understands GET and POST.

Alpine fills a similar, smaller role for purely client-side state:

<div x-data="{ open: false }">
  <button @click="open = !open">Toggle</button>
  <div x-show="open">Content</div>
</div>

If Alpine fails to load here, the content is still visible — it just won’t toggle. That’s the whole philosophy in miniature: enhancement that fails safe.

Where progressive enhancement still meets resistance

The strongest version of the complaint is that modern applications are too complex for this approach to scale. I don’t think that holds up — GitHub is not a simple application and is built this way extensively — but it’s worth taking seriously rather than dismissing outright, because some interactions genuinely are client-state-heavy enough that layering doesn’t make sense (a drawing tool, a live collaborative editor). What’s true for most applications, though, including most of what gets built as a SPA by default, is that they’re forms and data display, which is precisely the problem HTML was built to solve.

Progressive enhancement, utility-first CSS’s alternatives, and the case against SPAs by default all point the same direction: start from the primitive that already does the job, and add only what genuinely improves on it. The last article in this series asks what that means for how teams are structured around this work — specifically, whether the frontend/backend split still earns its cost once the technical gap between the two narrows.
entry.summary: Progressive enhancement is unfashionable, but starting from working HTML and layering on JavaScript still produces more resilient applications.

entry.title: The CSS Conundrum: Why Utility Classes Are Not The Answer

link.title: The CSS Conundrum: Why Utility Classes Are Not The Answer

entry.content:
The previous two articles in this series argued for pulling web development back toward hypertext and away from unnecessary client-side architecture. This one covers a parallel trend in styling: the rise of utility-first CSS, TailwindCSS in particular, and the broader habit of embedding presentation directly in markup.

The problems Tailwind actually solves

Traditional CSS has real failure modes, and it’s worth naming them honestly before arguing against the fix. Selectors are globally scoped, so two developers can collide on a class name without realising it. The cascade, useful as it is, makes it easy to produce specificity fights nobody can trace back to their source. Large stylesheets accumulate dead rules nobody’s confident enough to delete. Utility-first frameworks solve all of this by sidestepping it: a class like bg-blue-500 can never collide, can never be overridden unexpectedly, and is either used on the page or it isn’t.

That’s a real trade, not a fake one. The question is what you give up to make it.

What gets lost

Compare these two versions of the same component:

<div class="flex flex-col md:flex-row justify-between items-center p-4 bg-gray-100 rounded-lg shadow-md">
  <div class="flex items-center mb-4 md:mb-0">
    <img class="w-10 h-10 rounded-full mr-4" src="avatar.jpg" alt="User avatar">
    <div>
      <h3 class="text-lg font-medium text-gray-900">User Name</h3>
      <p class="text-sm text-gray-500">User Title</p>
    </div>
  </div>
  <button class="bg-blue-500 hover:bg-blue-700 text-white font-bold py-2 px-4 rounded">
    Follow
  </button>
</div>

<div class="user-card">
  <div class="user-profile">
    <img class="avatar" src="avatar.jpg" alt="User avatar">
    <div class="user-info">
      <h3 class="name">User Name</h3>
      <p class="title">User Title</p>
    </div>
  </div>
  <button class="follow-button">Follow</button>
</div>

The first tells you nothing about what the component is until you’ve parsed every class on every element. The second tells you in one glance: a user card, with a profile and a follow button. That’s not a style preference — semantic markup is supposed to describe structure, and the utility-class version has given that job up entirely in exchange for the collision-safety described above.

The maintainability cost follows from the same trade. If a design system decision changes — say, standard button padding — the semantic version changes one rule. The utility version means grepping every file that happens to use that combination of classes and hoping you found them all. Responsive variants make this worse before they make it better: md:flex-row and md:mb-0 scattered through markup is exactly the kind of noise that semantic class names were invented to hide.

The usual justification is colocation — keeping everything about a component in one file so there’s nowhere else to look. But colocation and coupling are the same thing described from two different angles. Keeping style and markup in one file doesn’t eliminate the need for consistency, it just means every place that needs it has to restate it, which is worse for consistency, not better.

What CSS was actually for

The cascade, inheritance, and specificity exist to let presentation be defined once and applied broadly, and to let it change in one place when the underlying intent changes. That’s not an accident of the spec; it’s the reason it’s called Cascading Style Sheets rather than Per-Element Style Attributes. Utility classes don’t improve on that model — they opt out of it, in favour of a programmatic style closer to inline styling, dressed up as classes.

Where I’d actually land

None of this is an argument for the stylesheet chaos that made Tailwind attractive in the first place. CSS Modules give you real scoping without the global-namespace risk. Sass or plain CSS with sensible partials and variables give you the cascade back without reintroducing the collision problem. CSS custom properties cover most of what people reach for a JavaScript-driven design-token system to do. BEM, applied with some discipline, gives markup back its semantics while still keeping class names predictable. All four solve the real problems that made utility classes look necessary, without giving up what semantic HTML and the cascade are for.

The next article in this series moves from CSS to a principle that both of the previous two implicitly depend on: progressive enhancement, and why building up from working HTML is still the right default even when a page ends up fully interactive.
entry.summary: Utility-first CSS solved real problems with the cascade, but at the cost of the separation between structure and presentation.

entry.title: HyperText and HTML: Why SPAs Are Dead

link.title: HyperText and HTML: Why SPAs Are Dead

entry.content:
The first article in this series set out my general complaint: that modern web development defaults to client-side complexity for problems that don’t need it. This one is about the specific case of single-page applications, and about why I think the pendulum is already swinging back, whether or not the industry has noticed yet.

Why SPAs happened

The rise of the SPA wasn’t an accident or a fad. Around 2010–2015 several things arrived at once: smartphones set an expectation for app-like interaction, browser APIs matured enough to support it, JavaScript engines got fast enough to make it tolerable, and React gave teams a component model that solved a genuine organisational problem — how a dozen people work on one UI without constantly colliding. For a while, these applications solved real problems: rich interaction without full page reloads, and a clean separation that let frontend and backend teams scale independently.

The costs took longer to show up than the benefits did.

What it costs

Open the dependency tree of a moderately complex React application and you’ll typically find a bundler, a transpiler, a state management library, a router, a form library, a data-fetching layer, and a component-testing framework — each one solving a real problem in isolation, and each one adding to a stack of complexity that doesn’t exist at all when HTML is rendered on the server. None of these tools are badly designed. The complexity isn’t a bug in any one of them; it’s the sum of needing all of them at once to do what a server used to do by itself.

The deeper issue is what I’d call the JSON API fallacy: the assumption that a backend should serve JSON even when it has exactly one consumer, the frontend of the same application. The typical SPA request looks like this — browser loads a near-empty HTML shell, JavaScript executes, JavaScript fetches JSON, JavaScript turns that JSON into HTML, and only then does the user see anything. A server rendering the page directly skips three of those four steps. The JSON step only earns its complexity when there’s a second consumer of the API — a mobile app, a third party — that actually needs it. Most CRUD applications don’t have one.

That fallacy also reinforces the frontend/backend split I mentioned in the first article: a JSON API is a contract, and contracts have to be negotiated, documented, and renegotiated every time the product changes. A team that didn’t need the contract in the first place doesn’t pay that cost.

What HTMX actually does

HTMX is interesting because it doesn’t propose an alternative architecture — it extends the one the browser already has.

<button hx-post="/submit" hx-target="#response-div">
  Submit
</button>
<div id="response-div"></div>

Two attributes turn a button into an asynchronous form submission that replaces the contents of a target element with whatever HTML the server sends back. No JSON, no client-side templating, no state to keep in sync between a store and the DOM — the server still owns the rendering, HTMX just gives it a way to update part of a page instead of the whole thing. It’s the same request/response model the web has always had, with slightly finer control over where the response lands.

Where SPAs still make sense

I don’t think this argument extends to every application. Offline-first tools, design and drawing applications, games — anything where the state genuinely lives on the client and the server is secondary — are legitimately served by a client-heavy architecture. What I’m arguing against is the default, not the exception: most dashboards, content sites, and CRUD applications don’t have offline requirements or client-side state worth the name, and building them as SPAs anyway is solving a problem the project doesn’t have.

What this means for frontend work

The obvious objection is that a lot of careers are built on frontend frameworks, and simplifying the default architecture threatens that. I think this gets the causality backwards: some of the complexity in frontend tooling exists because the specialisation needs defending, not because the problems demand it. But that doesn’t mean frontend expertise disappears — accessibility, animation, layout, and genuinely interactive client-side behaviour are still hard, specialist problems. What changes is that frontend developers would be solving those problems instead of re-implementing server rendering in the browser.

Pulling the architecture back toward hypertext doesn’t shrink what frontend developers do. It moves the boundary between frontend and backend from a JSON contract to a shared page, which is the thread I’ll pick back up in the last article in this series, on team structure.

The next article is CSS, and specifically what utility-first frameworks like Tailwind get right and where I think they go wrong.
entry.summary: Why single-page applications solved real problems for a time, and why HTML plus HTMX now solves most of the same problems more simply.
